title: Psalm 147: The God of the Stars Heals the Brokenhearted
summary: A hymn in three movements calling God's people to praise the LORD who rebuilds Jerusalem, gathers exiles, heals the brokenhearted, counts the stars, feeds the ravens, sends snow and thaw, and has given his word to Israel. Each movement sets God's power over creation beside his tender care for the lowly and his special gift to his people.
story: Psalm 147 is the second of the five psalms (146 to 150) that close the Psalter, each of which begins and ends with “Hallelujah”, meaning praise the LORD. After a book full of laments, pleas from exile, and hard questions about God's promises, the collection ends in sustained praise. Psalm 146 praised God as the helper of the oppressed; Psalm 147 narrows the focus to Jerusalem and Israel, the city being rebuilt and the scattered people coming home, while keeping the whole created world in view. It hands the reader on to Psalm 148, where the praise widens to heaven and earth.
historical:
The psalm has no superscription, no author, and no occasion named in a heading. Its content gives clues. The LORD “builds up Jerusalem; He gathers the exiles of Israel” (verse 2), and he “strengthens the bars of your gates” (verse 13). These lines fit most naturally after the Babylonian exile, when Jews returned from Babylon following Cyrus's decree of 539/538 BC and slowly rebuilt the temple and, in the time of Nehemiah in the fifth century BC, the walls of the city. Many scholars connect the psalm with that period, and some specifically with the dedication of Nehemiah's walls, though that exact link can't be proven. Others note that the language of building Jerusalem and gathering the outcasts also appears in older prophetic hope and could be sung at other times.

The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, the Septuagint, treats verses 1 to 11 and 12 to 20 as two separate psalms, which is one reason Psalm numbering differs between Greek-based and Hebrew-based traditions in this part of the book. The Hebrew text treats it as one psalm, and it reads well as a unity framed by Hallelujah at both ends.
cultural:
Several images would have spoken directly to the first singers. Horses were the tanks of the ancient world, the prized military asset of kings, and Israel's law warned its king not to multiply them (Deuteronomy 17:16). When the psalm says God “does not delight in the strength of the horse” (verse 10), it echoes a theme found also in Psalms 20 and 33: security does not come from military strength. City gates with heavy bars were a town's defense, and peace at the borders and fine wheat in the storehouses were the concrete marks of blessing in an agricultural society exposed to raids and drought.

The weather in verses 16 to 18 is also real to the land. Snow, frost, and hail do fall in the hill country of Judah and on Jerusalem in winter, sometimes heavily, and the spring thaw sends water running down the valleys. Neighboring peoples credited storm and rain to gods like Baal; the psalm credits them to the word of the LORD alone. The young ravens of verse 9 appear again in Job 38:41 as creatures that cry to God for food, a small picture of his care for things no one else notices.
literary: The psalm is a hymn with three stanzas, each opening with a fresh call to praise: verse 1 (“How good it is to sing praises to our God”), verse 7 (“Sing to the LORD with thanksgiving”), and verse 12 (“Exalt the LORD, O Jerusalem”). Each stanza then gives the reasons, often with participles describing what God habitually does: builds, gathers, heals, counts, covers, prepares, sends. The poem constantly moves between the cosmic and the personal. The God who numbers the stars in verse 4 is the one who binds wounds in verse 3; the God who commands snow and hail in verses 15 to 18 is the one who speaks his statutes to Jacob in verse 19. His “word” runs through the third stanza as both the power that governs weather and the revelation given to Israel, tying creation and covenant together.

outline.t: Praise the God who rebuilds, heals, and numbers the stars
Praise the God who feeds creation and delights in those who fear him
Praise the God whose word rules the weather and was given to Israel

doctrines.note: God is not only the maker of the world but its constant sustainer: he covers the sky with clouds, prepares rain, grows grass, feeds animals, and sends and melts the snow. Nothing in the weather or the food chain runs apart from his word.

The psalm pairs God's greatness with his tenderness. His understanding has no limit and he names every star, yet he stoops to heal the brokenhearted and sustain the humble. His power is never cold, and his care is never weak.

Verses 19 and 20 distinguish God's word in creation, which all nations experience, from his word given to Israel as statutes and judgments. The same God speaks through both, but the covenant word is a particular gift to a particular people.

words.note: Halal, to praise. The verb gives us Hallelujah, which joins a plural command, praise, to Yah, a short form of God's name. It opens and closes this psalm and each of the Psalter's final five. The Hebrew title of the whole book, Tehillim, comes from the same root: the book of praises.

Rapha, to heal. The word covers physical healing, the repair of broken things, and the restoring of a wounded people. In verse 3 it is paired with binding up wounds, the image of a physician dressing an injury. The LORD called himself Israel's healer at Exodus 15:26, and here that healing reaches the brokenhearted, those crushed by loss and exile.

Chesed, loving devotion. This is the loyal, committed love God shows within his covenant, often translated steadfast love or lovingkindness. In verse 11 the LORD takes pleasure not in strong legs or horses but in those who wait with hope on his chesed, trusting his faithful character rather than their own strength.

christ: Several lines of this psalm find their fullest expression in Jesus, though the psalm itself speaks of God's acts for Israel rather than predicting a Messiah. The God who heals the brokenhearted is the God whose Servant in Isaiah 61:1 is sent to bind them up, the passage Jesus read in the synagogue at Nazareth and said was fulfilled in him (Luke 4:18-21). The gathering of Israel's exiles becomes, in John 11:52, Jesus dying to gather into one the scattered children of God. And the word that runs swiftly across the earth takes on new depth in John 1, where the Word through whom all things were made becomes flesh. Psalm 147 closes with Israel's unique gift of God's word; the New Testament tells how that word went out to every nation through Christ.

hard.q: Why does the psalm celebrate that God gave his law to Israel and to no other nation?
hard.a: Verse 20 can sound like favoritism. The Old Testament is clear that God chose Israel, not because it was greater or better than other peoples (Deuteronomy 7:7-8), but out of his love and for a purpose: through Abraham's family all the families of the earth were to be blessed (Genesis 12:3). The psalm celebrates a privilege, not a superiority, and the same Psalter repeatedly calls the nations to praise the LORD (Psalms 67, 96, 117, and 148). Paul makes a similar point in Romans 3:2, that the Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God, a gift held in trust for the world. Christians read verse 20 as a stage in the story rather than its end: the particular gift to Israel was the means by which the knowledge of God would reach everyone.

questions: The psalm places God's naming of the stars right beside his healing of the brokenhearted. Which of these is harder for you to believe about God, and why?
Verses 10 and 11 say God is not impressed by strength but by those who hope in his loving devotion. What are the horses and strong legs you are tempted to trust?
How might noticing God's hand in ordinary weather, food, and seasons change the way you pray and give thanks?
